facts.statement: In 1974, Ostrom realized that the bone he had previously identified as a pubis was actually a coracoid, a shoulder element.
facts.quote: In 1974, Ostrom published another monograph on the shoulder of Deinonychus in which he realized that the pubis that he had described was actually a coracoid—a shoulder element

facts.statement: Gerald Grellet-Tinner and Peter Makovicky examined unprepared blocks in 2000 and found overlooked features.
facts.quote: An examination of these unprepared blocks by Gerald Grellet-Tinner and Peter Makovicky in 2000 revealed an interesting, overlooked feature

facts.statement: Bones previously identified as ossified tendons were found to actually be gastralia, or abdominal ribs.
facts.quote: Several long, thin bones identified on the blocks as ossified tendons (structures that helped stiffen the tail of Deinonychus) turned out to actually represent gastralia (abdominal ribs)

facts.statement: The contact between an eggshell and gastralia suggests Deinonychus may have brooded its eggs.
facts.quote: Moreover, the external surface of one eggshell was found in close contact with the gastralia suggesting that Deinonychus might have brooded its eggs

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Deinonychus used body heat for egg incubation, indicating endothermy similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: This implies that Deinonychus used body heat transfer as a mechanism for egg incubation, and indicates an endothermy similar to modern birds

facts.statement: A study by Gregory Erickson found that the individual specimen was 13 or 14 years old when it died and had reached full growth.
facts.quote: Further study by Gregory Erickson and colleagues finds that this individual was 13 or 14 years old at death and its growth had plateaued

facts.statement: John Ostrom described Deinonychus in 1969, an event considered the most important single discovery in mid-20th-century dinosaur paleontology.
facts.quote: Ostrom's description of Deinonychus in 1969 has been described as the most important single discovery of dinosaur paleontology in the mid-20th century.

facts.statement: The discovery of Deinonychus as an active, agile predator led to speculation that some dinosaurs were warm-blooded.
facts.quote: The discovery of this clearly active, agile predator did much to change the scientific (and popular) conception of dinosaurs and opened the door to speculation that some dinosaurs may have been warm-blooded.

facts.statement: John Ostrom revived the hypothesis that birds descended from dinosaurs after noting similarities between Deinonychus forefeet and bird feet.
facts.quote: Ostrom noted similarities between the forefeet of Deinonychus and that of birds, an observation which led him to revive the hypothesis that birds are descended from dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Deinonychus had powerful jaws lined with approximately seventy curved, blade-like teeth.
facts.quote: The skull was equipped with powerful jaws lined with around seventy curved, blade-like teeth.

facts.statement: Deinonychus possessed large hands with three claws on each forelimb.
facts.quote: Deinonychus possessed large "hands" (manus) with three claws on each forelimb.

facts.statement: No skin impressions have ever been found associated with Deinonychus fossils.
facts.quote: No skin impressions have ever been found in association with fossils of Deinonychus.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that Deinonychus and other dromaeosaurids were covered in feathers.
facts.quote: Nonetheless, the evidence suggests that the Dromaeosauridae, including Deinonychus, had feathers.

facts.statement: Deinonychus and Velociraptor form a clade called Velociraptorinae.
facts.quote: The clade they form is called Velociraptorinae.

facts.statement: A 2022 study reclassified Deinonychus as a basal member of Dromaeosaurinae.
facts.quote: A study in 2022, however, reclassified Deinonychus as a basal member of Dromaeosaurinae again.

facts.statement: In 2009, Manning and colleagues suggested dromaeosaur claw tips functioned as puncture and gripping elements while the expanded rear portion transferred load stress.
facts.quote: In 2009, Manning and colleagues interpreted dromaeosaur claw tips as functioning as a puncture and gripping element, whereas the expanded rear portion of the claw transferred load stress through the structure.

facts.statement: Manning and colleagues argued that the anatomy of dromaeosaur feet and hands supported prey capture, grappling, and climbing functions.
facts.quote: They argue that the anatomy, form, and function of the foot's recurved digit II and hand claws of dromaeosaurs support a prey capture/grappling/climbing function.

facts.statement: In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues proposed a new method for how Deinonychus captured and restrained prey.
facts.quote: In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues suggested a new method by which Deinonychus and other dromaeosaurs may have captured and restrained prey.

facts.statement: The 'raptor prey restraint' (RPR) model proposes Deinonychus killed prey by leaping on it, pinning it with body weight, and gripping it with large sickle-shaped claws, similar to accipitrid birds.
facts.quote: This model, known as the "raptor prey restraint" (RPR) model of predation, proposes that Deinonychus killed its prey in a manner very similar to extant accipitrid birds of prey: by leaping onto its quarry, pinning it under its body weight, and gripping it tightly with the large, sickle-shaped claws.

facts.statement: Fowler found dromaeosaur feet and legs most closely resemble eagles and hawks, particularly regarding an enlarged second claw and grasping motion.
facts.quote: Fowler found that the feet and legs of dromaeosaurs most closely resemble those of eagles and hawks, especially in terms of having an enlarged second claw and a similar range of grasping motion.

facts.statement: In 2020, Powers and colleagues suggested Deinonychus specialized on larger prey based on its short and deep maxilla resembling short-snouted canids.
facts.quote: In 2020, Powers and colleagues analyzed the snout morphology of dromaeosaurids from North America and Asia, their findings suggest that the maxilla of Deinonychus was short and deep, resembling that of short-snouted canids, suggesting that Deinonychus specialized on larger prey.

facts.statement: A 2022 study using a Deinonychus skull calculated a bite force of 706 newtons.
facts.quote: A recent 2022 study used a Deinonychus skull for their estimate and calculated 706 N.

facts.statement: Deinonychus likely used its strong bite force for defense or capturing prey rather than for feeding.
facts.quote: Instead, they probably used their strong bite force for defense or to capture prey, rather than for feeding.

facts.statement: Anatomical and trackway evidence indicates Deinonychus held its sickle talon off the ground while walking on its third and fourth toes.
facts.quote: There is anatomical and trackway evidence that this talon was held up off the ground while the dinosaur walked on the third and fourth toes.

facts.statement: Ostrom suggested Deinonychus could kick with its sickle claw to cut and slash prey, with some researchers proposing it was used to disembowel large ceratopsians.
facts.quote: Ostrom suggested that Deinonychus could kick with the sickle claw to cut and slash at its prey. Some researchers even suggested that the talon was used to disembowel large ceratopsian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Other studies suggest Deinonychus sickle claws were used to deliver small stabs rather than to slash.
facts.quote: Other studies have suggested that the sickle claws were not used to slash but rather to deliver small stabs to the victim.

facts.statement: In 2005, Manning and colleagues tested a robotic replica of Deinonychus striking a pig carcass and found the talons made only shallow punctures.
facts.quote: In 2005, Manning and colleagues ran tests on a robotic replica that precisely matched the anatomy of Deinonychus and Velociraptor, and used hydraulic rams to make the robot strike a pig carcass.

facts.statement: Manning and colleagues suggested Deinonychus talons were more effective for climbing than for dealing killing blows.
facts.quote: The authors suggested that the talons would have been more effective in climbing than in dealing killing blows.

facts.statement: A 2011 study suggested Deinonychus used its sickle claw to pin down prey while biting rather than as a slashing weapon.
facts.quote: In 2011, a study suggested that the sickle claw would likely have been used to pin down prey while biting it, rather than as a slashing weapon.

facts.statement: In 2002, Ken Carpenter confirmed that Deinonychus forelimbs were likely used for grasping prey due to their length allowing greater reach.
facts.quote: Biomechanical studies by Ken Carpenter in 2002 confirmed that the most likely function of the forelimbs in predation was grasping, as their great lengths would have permitted longer reach than for most other theropods.

facts.statement: A 2006 study by Phil Senter suggested Deinonychus could use its forelimbs to clutch objects against its chest.
facts.quote: Studies by Phil Senter in 2006 indicated that Deinonychus forelimbs could be used not only for grasping, but also for clutching objects towards the chest.

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined 43 hand bones and 52 foot bones of Deinonychus and found no signs of stress fractures.
facts.quote: In a 2001 study conducted by Bruce Rothschild and other paleontologists, 43 hand bones and 52 foot bones referred to Deinonychus were examined for signs of stress fracture; none were found.

facts.statement: The specimen YPM 5205 possesses a healed fracture on the second phalanx of the second toe.
facts.quote: The second phalanx of the second toe in the specimen YPM 5205 has a healed fracture.

facts.statement: Research by Parsons and Parsons indicates that juvenile and sub-adult Deinonychus exhibit morphological differences compared to adults.
facts.quote: Parsons and Parsons have shown that juvenile and sub-adult specimens of Deinonychus display some morphological differences from the adults.

facts.statement: Parsons and Parsons hypothesized that juvenile Deinonychus had more curved claws to aid tree climbing, which straightened as the animals aged and became terrestrial.
facts.quote: Parsons and Parsons have suggested that the claw curvature (which Ostrom [1976] had already shown was different between specimens) maybe was greater for juvenile Deinonychus, as this could help it climb in trees, and that the claws became straighter as the animal became older and started to live solely on the ground.

facts.statement: A 2015 analysis of immature fossils suggested that the mobile shoulder joint of young Deinonychus might have allowed for some form of flight.
facts.quote: In a 2015 paper, it was reported after further analysis of immature fossils that the open and mobile nature of the shoulder joint might have meant that young Deinonychus were capable of some form of flight.

facts.statement: A 2016 study by Scott Persons IV and Currie found Deinonychus scored -2.2 on cursoriality indices, suggesting it could not maintain high speeds for long periods.
facts.quote: In 2016, Scott Persons IV and Currie examined the limb proportion of numerous theropods and found Dromaeosaurids weren't cursorial animals due to their low CLP scores, with Deinonychus scoring -2.2, suggesting they couldn't maintain high speeds for extended periods of time.
